content.content:
- F-385 **The class loader chooses a compiled call's opcode from the owner's class file, without loading the owner.** Where an instantiated template calls a method by `invokeinterface` on a type that becomes a plain class name, `MethodInstantiater.visitMethodInsn` reads `ACC_INTERFACE` from the class file that the loader would define for that name, and uses `invokevirtual` for a class (`runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java`). So an object that lists a self-typed trait first, whose JVM superclass is that trait's default methods at the object, runs a default body that calls a method on a value of the self-type parameter (row 1052, fixed). Two limits, by reading, neither measured nor held by a test. The read keeps no cache, unlike the loader's lookup of generic expansions beside it, so each such call site of each expansion reads a class file. A class that the loader generates, such as a generic object's, has no class file, so the loader loads it as before, and a generic object that lists a self-typed trait first may still fail as row 1052 did. Test: `compiler_tests/SelfTypeParameterReceiverRun`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-self-arm-closure/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why", item 3; `reviews/batch-33-review.md`, "2. The decisions that landed at a default".

- F-386 **A dotted call on a value whose static type is an intersection in which no conjunct lies below the others compiles as a call on the conjunct that has the declaration the checker chose.** Such a type comes from a call typed by the intersection of its candidates' return types (P-60) and from a `typecase` binder whose arm's type neither lies below nor above the selector's. The code generator casts the receiver to that conjunct, the most specific where several qualify, else the first in the intersection's order; the value's own method runs, as under walk. Where the conjuncts are two instances of one generic trait, as `List[\E\] ∩ List[\T\]` in the one library's `app`, the choice changes no answer, by reading: no type extends two instances of one generic trait (P-43, the exclusion rule), so such a value exists only where `E` and `T` are one type; no test calls such a method. A getter goes to a conjunct whose method of that name takes no argument; a method overloaded across the conjuncts and a generic method compile too. On the one library this emits `__filter`. The checker refuses a method of a type parameter's bound on such a value where a conjunct is the parameter (row 1072). Tests: `compiler_tests/CoverageReturnMethodCall.test`, `compiler_tests/TypecaseBinderMethodCall.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-intersection-receiver/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why" and "5. Programs run old against new".

- F-387 **The compiled path compiles a primary whose math items all apply in turn to its front: `x[5]^2` is `(x[5])^2` and `g[1][2]` is `(g[1])[2]`; and a subscript as a math item before a tightly juxtaposed item: `x[5]k` is `(x[5]) k`.** The checker checks the one application that the reassociation leaves, at the expected type, and writes each subscript as a call of the subscript operator's method, as the desugaring before it writes every other subscript (`scala_src/typechecker/impls/Operators.scala`). Walk runs these forms too (F-398), so a program for both paths may write them unparenthesised. Test: `compiler_tests/SubscriptThenSuperscriptCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-small-gaps/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why", item 2.

- F-388 **The compiler's prelude declares its seven number types as value objects, whose classes the code generator writes over the run time's payload classes.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32` and `RR64` are `value object`s in `CompilerBuiltin`; each object's class extends the abstract payload class `compiler/runtimeValues/F<T>`, which holds the JVM value. Descriptors, stamped instances and the RTTI's `className()` name the type by the payload class, while the RTTI's class stays the object's, so that the type lies below its traits at run time; a dotted call casts its receiver to the object's class; `F<T>.make` reaches the object's class's `make` by the name that `LibraryNames` gives: the first set's names the prelude's seven, and under the selection the code generator writes the one library's seven over the same payload classes, whose names the second set's `LibraryNames` gives (F-396). So a program's object below a number type is refused at the compile, an overloading at `ZZ32` beside one at a program's trait is valid, a `typecase` clause at such a trait over a number is refused as unreachable (row 1081), and a number type named as a value does not compile (row 1082). Tests: `compiler_tests/NumberObjectsCompiled.test`, `compiler_tests/XXXNumberTypeExtendRefusedCompiled.test`, `compiler_tests/ComprisesMeetGenericTrait.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-number-payload-objects/REPORT.md`, "The design as built (a point to report)"; `compile-ladder/rung-first-run-one-library/REPORT.md`, "The design as built (a point to report)".

- F-389 **The code generator names the class of a function expression or a local function by its component and its source span, and a later one at a span already named takes the name with `#2`, `#3`, in the order in which the code generator meets them.** Closures share a span in these forms: the thunk that a conditional operator, such as `OR:`, makes of its right operand, and the outer closure `fn (reduction, unit) => ...` of a reduction that is that operand; the thunk that a binding `if`, `if x <- m then ... else ... end`, makes of its else part, where the else part is a reduction; and the function expression that an arrow coercion wraps around a function expression argument. In each, the thunk or the wrapper is met first and keeps the plain name. The names are made once per compile of a component (`NamingCzar.gensymArrowClassName`, `CodeGen.closureClassNames`), so they are the same from compile to compile and under another identity-hash mode, such as `-XX:hashCode=0`. So F-34's measure emits the one library's `LexicographicOrder`. Tests: `compiler_tests/ConditionalReductionCompiled.test`, `compiler_tests/ArrowCoercionFnExprCompiled.test`, `one_library_tests/OneLibraryConditionalReduction.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-closure-name-once/REPORT.md`, "4. The naming as built".

- F-397 **A numeral with a radix point keeps its digits as written in the node that both paths read, so its digit count `n` counts its leading zeros: `00.5` is `RadixPointNumeral[\3, 1, 10, 5\]`.** It builds P-174's digit count. `ExprFactory.makeFloatLiteralExpr` removes only apostrophes and U+202F from the numeral's text (`nodes_util/ExprFactory.java:1637-1638`), as `makeIntLiteralExpr` does, and `NumeralNumbers.of` counts `n` from that text for the checker and for walk (`nodes_util/NumeralNumbers.java:71-100`); the value, `m` and `v` are read as before. A message that quotes the numeral shows it as written. A folded `MIN`, `MAX` or `|x|` whose answer is a written radix-point operand keeps that operand's text, so its numeral type in a checker message counts the operand's zeros; a folded `+` takes its value's digits. This rule for folded constants is a worker's choice, not a decision of the curator; no coercion reads a folded constant's numbers (P-174). Tests: `tests/RadixPointLeadingZerosWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/RadixPointLeadingZerosCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-radix-point-leading-zeros/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Every reader of the node's text, and what it now sees".

- F-398 **Walk applies a subscript that is a math item with all its indices, and binds a tuple binding's names from one run of its right side.** `x[5]^2` is `(x[5])^2`, `m[3,7]^2` is `(m[3,7])^2`, `g[3][7]` is `(g[3])[7]` and `x[5]k` is `(x[5]) k` under walk as on the compiled path (F-387): `evalAndInvokeMethod`, the one helper of `mathItemApplication`, evaluates every index as `forSubscriptExpr` does (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:1069-1071`). A tuple binding at the top level or as a field of an object or object expression runs its right side once: a tuple expression of as many elements as names binds each name to its own element, and any other right side binds a temporary declared at the names' types, which each name reads through the desugarer's own `Local` or `Member` reference (`interpreter/rewrite/DesugarerVisitor.java:854`, `:868-877`, `:878-893`, `:897`), as the compiled path does (F-369); a numeral converts to its name's declared type, as at a single binding. Where such a right side does not convert to the names' types, walk's message names the temporary, not the name, as 'Type mismatch binding (5,6) ... to *tuple_<span> (type (NN32,String))'; this message is a worker's choice, not a decision of the curator. An array literal inside a right side that is not a tuple expression, bound at an array type, is not built and stops at load (row 1105). So a program for both paths writes these forms unparenthesised, and binds a call's tuple to names directly. Tests: `tests/SubscriptThenSuperscriptWalk.fss`, `tests/TopLevelTupleBindingOnceWalk.fss`, `tests/FieldTupleBindingOnceWalk.fss`, `tests/TupleBindingNumeralTypesWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-subscript-tuple-binding/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Old against new".

- F-399 **The dispatch method of a trait's or an object's functional method reads each argument at its own local, wherever self stands.** The method is an instance method of the receiver's class, with self in local 0 and the other arguments after it in their order. `OverloadSet.argumentLocal`, overridden in `ForTraitOrObject`, gives an argument before self's place the local after its own place, for the type tests and the casts alike (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:2357-2363`, `:2495-2508`, `:1538`, `:1876`). A call reaches the dispatch method where the declaration that the top-level dispatch of the name chooses has a more specific one below it in the type, as an inherited one does; a declaration of the type with none below it is called at its exact signature, its body. It does not reach two forms: a generic functional method overloaded beside a plain one, on which the code generator stops first (row 724), and a generic functional method with self not first, which dies at another site (row 594). So an object or trait may overload an inherited functional method with self anywhere. Tests: `compiler_tests/FunctionalMethodOverloadSelfLast`, `FunctionalMethodCoverSelfSecond`, `FunctionalMethodSelfSecondReceiverTested`, `FunctionalMethodMeetNarrowedSelfNotFirst`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-self-not-first-dispatch/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- F-400 **The code generator compiles the modifier `override` by the checker's table of what an override keeps from being inherited, and the checker refuses an `override` that overrides nothing.** A trait's or an object's class holds the override and, at each hidden declaration's JVM signature, a bridge that runs it; no method runs the hidden declaration, and a dispatch over the override and the declarations of its name that it does not override is still written (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1798-1812`, `overriddenNotProvided`; `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1224-1237`, `overrideBridges`; `:1476-1484`, `dumpOverloadedMethodChaining`). The checker refuses an `override` that appears in no overriding pair of `providedAndOverridden`, equal parameter types included, as the traits chapter and walk do: 'Invalid override of f in object B: ... has the modifier override and does not override any inherited declaration.' (`scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:424`, `:763-789`). Two forms stay code-generator walls: an override of or by a method with static parameters of its own, and one in a generic type whose parameter types name a static parameter (row 1106). The checker refuses an override that overrides a declaration inherited under a conditional extension only by the clause's bound, which walk runs (row 1107), and does not check an override in an object expression (row 1108). Under walk an object's override hides every inherited declaration of its name (row 1109). So a program may write `override` on the compiled path wherever no static parameter is involved. Tests: `compiler_tests/OverrideModifierCodeGeneration`, `OverrideBridgesCompiled`, `XXXOverrideNothingCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-override-compiled/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- F-401 **An exit out of an `atomic` block commits the block's transaction and keeps its writes, on both paths.** Compiled, the block's handler `BaseTask.leaveTransaction` commits on a `LabelExit` as `endTransaction` does at a normal end (`runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:303-309`); walk's `FortressTaskRunner.doItOnce` commits on a `LabelException` as at a normal end (`interpreter/evaluator/tasks/FortressTaskRunner.java:133-141`). A commit that fails runs the block again, as at a normal end, and an exception other than an exit still discards the writes. A nested block's commit hands its writes to the outer one, whose commit on the same exit stores them. Neither path tells an exit to an enclosing label from one to a label block that has completed, so such a late exit also commits the atomic blocks it passes (row 1041). Under walk an exit or an exception out of a `tryatomic` block that no `atomic` block encloses is wrapped in a `RuntimeException` and reaches neither its label nor a `catch` (rows 1110 and 1111). So a program may exit out of an atomic block (`Specification/basic/expressions/atomic.tex:59-63`). Tests: `tests/ExitOutOfAtomicWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/ExitOutOfAtomicCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-exit-out-of-atomic/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "The tests: failing on the base, passing after".

- F-402 **Both paths fold two natural numerals of one radix joined by `||` into one natural numeral, as the constant chapter says.** So `deadc_16 || 0de_16` is `deadc0de_16` before the checker: its digits are both numerals' digits in order, leading zeros kept (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/constant.tex:80-82`; `compiler/desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java`), and the constant chapter's revision box states it. P-174 leaves out the binary chapter's numeral coercion and its `opr ||` with a numeral, and does not name this concatenation: folding it is a planner's default that rung F built (climb batch 29's fork F4, with rung T's text, fork T2), not a decision of the curator; the way not taken drops it, so that `deadc_16 || 0de_16` finds no `||`, as on the base under walk. Tests: `tests/NumeralFoldWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/LiteralFoldCompiled.test`, `NumeralFoldJUTest`. Detail: `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-29.md`, "The three points with no default on record", point 2.

- F-403 **The one library declares `EQV` (`≡`) and `NEQV` (`≢`) over two booleans, as top-level operators beside `<->`; walk and the compiled path under the one library run them, and on a program's own objects each is a type error.** `EQV`'s body is `if a then b else NOT b end`, which calls no `=`, and `NEQV`'s is `NOT (a EQV b)`, the specification's definition of `≢` (`Specification/basic-lib/Fortress.NegatedOperators.tex`). The specification and the compiler's prelude write both as methods of `Boolean`; the one library keeps its own form, top-level operators, for the boolean operators, within P-37; that form is a default of the batch's plan, which the curator has not decided. Under walk `a ≡ b` for two objects of a program's type stops at the call, 'Unification error: Closure/Constructor for EQV param 1 (a:Boolean) got arg Pt of type Pt', and compiled it is refused, 'Could not check call to operator EQV'. Under walk, a program that imports the APL experiments' `AplCore` gets its infix `≡` and prefix `≢` over `RR64` and arrays in one overload set with the library's two: its own calls give the values that they gave without the library's two, and `t ≡ f` and `t ≢ f` of two booleans print `false` and `true`. No gated program and no line of microGPT imports `AplCore`. That one overload set is the one that P-181 asks: every visible declaration of the name. Under walk an equivalence operator that nothing declares, as `APPROX`, still loads and stops at its call with an internal error (row 1118); the one library declares none of `Boolean`'s `⊕`, `⊼` and `⊽`, and no library `majority` (row 1121). Tests: `tests/BooleanEquivalenceWalk.fss`, `one_library_tests/OneLibraryBooleanEquivalence.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-boolean-equivalence/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Row 184's own program, and the other programs".

- F-405 **Walk runs the generic dotted methods of one name that a trait or an object declares together, each as its instance at symbolic static arguments.** An object takes each generic method of a name, alone or beside others of the name, with one symbolic instantiation for each name and, per static parameter, kind and bounds, with the method's own static parameters in the bounds compared by position, not by name (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Constructor.java`, `genericKey`): so an object's redeclaration of a trait's generic method at the same bounds under other names hides it, and two that differ in their bounds are overloads, except bounds that differ only in the api of a type of one simple name (row 1134). At load walk reads two such instances on their declared domains where one lies inside the other; a set of them whose overlap only a third covers is refused (row 1133), and so is, when an extending object's first instance is made, a nested pair of a generic trait's generic functional methods (row 780). An object that inherits two such methods of one name from two traits, neither more specific, with no declaration at their meet, loads and runs, where the Meet Rule refuses the set (row 1139). A call that writes no static argument infers them and dispatches among the instances, the inner declared domain first; a call that writes static arguments instantiates each generic method whose static parameters, by their number and kinds, take them, and chooses among those instances by the call's arguments, as a call of a top-level generic function does. A call on a receiver assumed at the trait stops (row 1126). Where a plain method shares the name with a generic one, a call that writes static arguments stops (row 744); of two generic functional methods of one name and one number of parameters, the second is never chosen (row 1123). Tests: `tests/GenericMethodOverloadArity.fss`, `GenericMethodOverloadSetWalk.fss`, `GenericOverloadStaticArgKindsWalk.fss`, `GenericMethodBoundsDifferWalk.fss`, whose object `Both` asserts walk's answers for row 1139's set, the departure. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-load-check-generic-numeral/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Programs run old against new"; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-bounds-tuple-numeral-type/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why".

- F-406 **A compiled setter's call passes its value at the field's type, and a compiled call of several declarations names an overload method that the class holds.** The code generator passes the value of `c.t := v`, which the desugarer makes a call with no arrow (the checker's type for a call), at the setter's parameter type at the receiver's instance (`CodeGen.setterParamType`), also on a receiver typed by a type variable whose bounds hold the setter, cast below self's trait where it has self's type (F-377). It writes the overload method that a call names where the checker leaves it several declarations, its set split with its principal member (`CodeGen.for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl`), and, where the call's arrow is not the principal member's, a method at the call's signature that passes its arguments on (`CodeGen.forwardToPrincipal`). The written method is a default of the batch's plan, and the forwarder a worker's choice beyond the plan; the other way was to make each call through the trait. The curator has decided neither. So `c.t := High`, `s.r := self` at a type that a `comprises` clause lists, `num(R)` beside a trait's `num(self)`, a call on `self` in such a trait, and a call that one declaration takes without coercion and another by a coercion run compiled; the one library's `FortressLibrary` holds the overload methods `numerator{...}` and `denominator{...}`. A comprised object's functional method at a narrower return type than its trait's type checks, since the signatures read `self` at the trait (F-408). Tests: `compiler_tests/VarFieldAssignedSubtypeRun`, `FunctionalMethodComprisedObject`, `ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall`, `CoercionAnyOverloadRungC`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-compiled-missing-methods/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why" and "5. Programs run on the old code and on the new".

- F-407 **A numeral coercion's four numbers convert where they stand, on both paths, a `ZZ` where nothing fixes a type.** It builds P-174's rule for a coercion's body, with P-173's conversion. Walk binds each as a static number whose default is a `ZZ` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java`), which converts where its place fixes a type as a folded constant does and is refused there when the place runs. The checker types it `ZZ`, keeps it so at a call that a declaration takes so, converts it where its place fixes a bounded number type, also in a result position of a join there, and refuses at the numeral's place a number that does not fit, for a coercion of the numeral's own component. The code generator converts it from the `ZZ`. So `ZZ32`'s coercion is `= v` and a byte type's `Byte(v)`. Two departures, both on the compiled path: a number that does not fit, in another component's coercion, is not refused statically (row 1131); a number at a call runs the declaration that takes a `ZZ` (row 1132). Tests: `tests/NumeralCoercionBodyWalk.fss`, `NumeralCoercionNumberRangeWalk.fss`, `NumeralCoercionNumberAtCallWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/NumeralCoercionBodyCompiled`, `XXXNumeralCoercionNumberRangeCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-coercion-body/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- F-162 **Citing `Specification/library/apis/*.tex` as an independent standard is circular.** The team says that the library part "is largely automatically generated from the API code" (`Specification/library/structure.tex:25-31`). The build renders these listings from the `.fsi` files of `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, and the listings are not in the tree. So a listing cannot justify an edit of an `.fsi` file: the edit changes the listing in the next built PDF. Cite the `.fsi` line. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` holds the rule.

- F-163 **Of the two copies of the specification, `Specification/` is the one to search and change; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is byte for byte the Working Draft of 2011-02-02, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 text.** `git diff --quiet 2f8b4331a:Specification c02fa44d0:Specification-1.0-frozen` succeeds; `2f8b4331a` is the team's last commit of the draft (2011-02-02). In the frozen copy, Appendix I, the changes appendix, is a stub that the team left; in `Specification/` it holds the revival's changes (P-96). `Specification/fortress.pdf` is a draft build, so the team's `\note` boxes print. A third text, the team's unfinished restart, is later on some topics (F-166). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` says how to cite and change each copy. Detail: `reviews/spec-change-form.md` sections 5 and 7.

- F-165 **The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, and `main` descends from `8fe1daa8f`, which copied a third-party Java 9 port onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`.** The port shares no history with this tree, and most of its 1,506 files are removed or redone. Of the port's code, only the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash still runs. `lineage.md` lists what can go with no change of behaviour: that fix, replaced by `clean-ladder`'s two-line repair, and the port's dead jars, dead files and cosmetic edits. The branch `clean-ladder` (`8332bd34f`) rebuilds on `a874948ac` without the port and never replaced `main`. Detail: `coordinator/lineage.md`, "The facts" (the fork, the graft and the port's files), and "Verification against Pavol's recollection (the same worker, re-briefed)", items "Working code" and "Verdict" (the running piece and what can go).

- F-166 **On the topics of its Types chapter, such as the exclusion rule and covariance, the team's latest word is the unfinished restart, not `Specification/`.** The restart, `Documentation/Specification/`, was never adopted. Its Types chapter restates the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" and adds `covariant`. On the rest of static parameters, and on traits beyond a stub, exceptions, components and the numeric library, `Specification/` is the only statement. Which text governs is the curator's: `Specification/` stays the standard, the Types chapter is cited beside it, and `covariant` is future work (P-25). The type group's POPL 2019 paper is later than both (F-271). Detail: `coordinator/spec-lineage.md` section 6 and its "Coordinator's check (2026-09-26)".

- F-167 **The specification states instantiation exclusion and keeps each example that the rule refuses, marked "Not allowed"; the calculi of Appendix A carry a callout that they predate the rule.** It builds P-97. It also bars a `where`-clause variable from an `extends` clause's static arguments. The covariance example, the empty list, the empty optional value and the root type `Object`'s algebraic supertraits each stand beside the library's shape, which runs on both paths except `Nothing[\String\]` on the compiled prelude (row 331). A subtrait of every instantiation stays as the counterexample that introduces the rule, and the internal appendix's refused examples get a callout each. The checker does not yet refuse two cases: an object that extends two instantiations that differ only in a `bool` argument (row 406), and one that extends two instantiations of one trait where one instantiation's argument is the object's own static parameter, such as `O[\nat n\] extends { Vec[\n\], Vec[\3\] }` (row 414). Detail and examples: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3; its section 4.2 (the calculi's callout).

- F-168 **The specification's number chapters describe the flat library, and its advanced chapter on rational quantities stays word for word under a callout that marks it superseded.** The eight number types are siblings under `Number` (F-131). They convert by the library's coercions (P-74), and every other conversion is explicit, such as `asFloat(x)`. The sign-refined types, such as positive ℚ, are gone; a program tests a value's sign at run time (P-80). ℚ holds +∞, −∞ and 0/0, and claims neither a field nor a total order. `QQ` extends the four algebraic traits that the library declares on it, `StandardPartialOrder`, `StandardMinMax`, `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, and their laws hold for the finite rationals. F-172 gives the integer chapter's rules. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md` section 3; `Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:245-250` (ℚ's traits); `Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex:14` (the callout).

- F-169 **The Working Draft never wrote static-argument inference, never named the type that a library gives an integer numeral, and never named a range's integer type; the specification's text on these is the revival's.** The Working Draft's inference chapter is a heading and notes. It described numeral types, such as `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`, and said that libraries define coercions from numerals to integers and rationals. But a note of its own leaves the numeral types' hierarchy undescribed, and it names no type that a library declares for a numeral. Its ranges section names no integer type. The later restart adds nothing on the three. So a citation of the specification on them cites the revival, not the team. The revised text states F-173's inference rule and F-170's ranges, and gives an integer numeral the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]`, its four numbers as static arguments (P-174). Detail: `reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/evidence-B.md` sections 1 and 2; `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:87-96` and `:132-148` (the note and the coercions); `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:146-161` (the callout on the numeral types).

- F-170 **The specification's ranges are over ℤ32, and its own ranges over wider integer types are respelled.** An integer numeral, and a `nat` or `int` parameter, used as an operand of an explicit range, such as `a` or `n` in `a#n`, converts to ℤ32 (row 485, fixed). An operand of any other integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter must have a wider integer type runs over a range of ℤ32 values and widens each element. The two examples that built `ZZ64` ranges run over ℤ32, and `ant testSpecData`, a gate step, runs both (F-114). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-ranges/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3; `Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex:42-60` and `:90-111`.

- F-171 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause as the restart's Types chapter does: every value of the trait is a value of a listed type.** So a trait or object that extends the closed trait must be below a listed type, with two exceptions. A trait with a `comprises` clause of its own may stay unlisted if each of its own listed types is below a listed type of the closed trait. A trait with static parameters may stay unlisted if at least one type extends it and every type that extends it is below a listed type. A listed type may be an instantiation at the trait's static parameters or `where`-clause variables. The text does not say whether a bare type variable may be listed; walk overflows its stack on one (row 407). The compiled checker departs in three ways: it checks only the closed trait's immediate subtypes (row 487), it reads the clause in the subtrait's own type-variable names (row 489), and it finds extenders by the simple text of a name (row 490). Whether the team's commented `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]` is valid is open (F-121). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md` section 2; `Specification/basic/traits.tex:246-269`.

- F-172 **The specification's integer chapter states the library's integer rules.** The getters `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` and `asZZ` keep the value or throw `IntegerOverflow`. `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the bits and throw nothing: `narrow` converts a `ZZ64` to `ZZ32`, and an `NN64` to `NN32`, by keeping the low 32 bits, so a value that does not fit wraps. `ZZ` has neither `narrow` nor `widen`. `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` work on the five integer types. On `ZZ` they are `shift`, which is exact at any count. On a fixed-size type, `LSHIFT` loses the bits shifted out and throws nothing. `GCD` and `LCM` are nonnegative, and one that a fixed-size type cannot hold throws `IntegerOverflow`. At a negative power, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 throws `DivisionByZero`, and any other base throws `IntegerOverflow`. The library follows the same power rule under walk; the compiled path's own library does not (F-263). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md` section 2; `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:39-98` (the conversions and the shifts) and `:562-574` (the power); `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:262-268` (`GCD` and `LCM`).

- F-173 **The specification's type-inference chapter states the rule that the compiled checker builds: the declaration is chosen first, then its static arguments are inferred.** It states P-46, P-48 and P-49. A type parameter that a parameter's declared type mentions inside another type, as `List[\T\]` mentions `T`, is fixed by the argument at that position. One that is the whole declared type of one or more parameters, as `T` is of `x: T`, and that nothing else fixes, takes the narrowest type, within its bounds, that every one of those arguments has or converts into: `ZZ64` for a `ZZ32` and an `NN32`. Where there is none, and no numeral settles the tie, it takes its bound, narrowed by what the call's expected type requires of the return type (P-48). So does a type parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes. Inference never gives a type parameter `BottomType`. The compiled path departs from the chapter in these ways, among others. Its prelude lacks the coercion of `NN32` into `ZZ64`, so a `ZZ32` and an `NN32` instantiate a type parameter at `ZZ`, not `ZZ64`; no callout names this (row 442, `compiler_tests/XXXInferPromoteNN32`). The callouts at `Specification/basic/inference.tex:285-347` and `:448-512` also give walk's departures, such as the return type `BottomType` that walk gives a function expression that declares none (row 587). Plain tests gate the rule for a type parameter that is a parameter's whole type, at its bound where no argument type is narrowest, on both paths: `compiler_tests/InferLone*` and `tests/InferLone*Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/REPORT.md` (the bound rule); `Specification/basic/inference.tex:45-125` (the chapter's rule).

- F-174 **The specification states the type group's 2011 overloading model: declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters, and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration over all its instances within its bounds.** It states P-45 and P-42. The section "Declarations with Static Parameters" states the OOPSLA 2011 paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet. It gives one more restriction as the compiled path's, not the language's. Where one generic declaration is more specific than another with as many static parameters, the two must declare them of the same kinds, position by position. Also, the more specific one's return type must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are matched by position, so the checker refuses an override whose return type reorders its static parameters (row 398, fixed). The section "Principles of Overloading" forbids overloading a functional whose single parameter's type is a type parameter with the bound `Any` written, as `T extends Any`. A type parameter with no `extends` clause, whose bound is also `Any`, is exempt. Both paths refuse such an overload: the checker in `OverloadingChecker.checkBoundAny`, and walk since row 534's fix. Neither path runs every set that the rules allow. Appendix I's entry "Overloading with static parameters" names the sets that each path fails. In row 1048, the checker refuses a generic declaration beside a plain one over a tuple of object types, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: (Circle, Circle)): (Circle, Circle)`. In row 537, the code generator fails on two generic declarations whose bounds differ. In row 539, walk refuses at load the 2019 paper's valid set over an array list and a list. In rows 779 and 780, walk fails on two generic functional methods one of whose declared domains lies inside the other's: in a trait or object without static parameters it refuses them at load, and in a trait with static parameters it stops with an error when an extending object's first instance is made. Detail: `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:134-150` and `:531-674`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 3 and 4.

- F-175 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values in every passage.** It builds P-60. Appendix I's entry "Traits with comprises clauses read at the level of values" records the change. A call whose argument's static type stands between two closed traits runs the declaration that covers its value. Where its declarations have no static parameters, its type is the intersection of its most specific declarations' return types. Appendix I names three places where the compiled path departs. The checker checks a `comprises` clause at the closed trait's immediate subtypes only (row 487). The checker refuses the Meet Rule's example for closed traits when its declarations have static parameters (row 546). The checker's verdict on an overload set can depend on the components compiled before it in the same JVM (row 547). Detail: `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3486-3681`, with the rows at `:1677` and `:3752-3755`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 8 and 9.

- F-176 **The specification allows arithmetic in a size, and two size arguments are identical when they are written alike once each operation whose operands are numerals is replaced by its value.** It states P-55. By the grammar, a size is a numeral, a name, a sum, a difference, a product, a power to a numeral or a name, or a bracketed size. So `2 3` and `6` are identical, but `s0 s1` and `s1 s0` are not. Two types are identical when they have the same name and identical static arguments, sizes compared this way. Two sizes are known to differ when they are two different numerals. A static parameter, or a size in which one occurs, is not known to differ from a numeral, since an instance may make them equal. F-146 gives the compiled checker, and F-222 walk's arithmetic. When walk infers a size parameter from a call's argument type, it matches a numeral and binds a name, and solves no size written as an operation: read in `IntNat.unifyStaticArg` (`interpreter/evaluator/types/IntNat.java:126-147`), and observed in row 767. Source: `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:49-62`; `Specification/appendices/grammars/concrete-syntax.tex:533-547` (`IntExpr`).

- F-223 **The specification's No Duplicates Rule is the papers' non-strict rule, and the compiled checker applies it, to functional methods wherever their `self` parameters stand, abstract ones included.** Two declarations of one name may not each be applicable to every call to which the other is, as in the type group's papers of 2011 and 2019 (P-26). The checker refuses such a pair, two functional methods at different `self` positions and an abstract functional method beside a concrete one among them: "There are multiple declarations of f with the same parameter type", naming the domain of the declaration written first. It checks symbolic operators too (F-281): `opr ||(self, y: S)` beside `opr ||(x: S, self)` in a trait `S` is refused, 'There are multiple declarations of || with the same parameter type: (S)'. Walk refuses at load such a pair of two generic declarations whose parameter types mention their static parameters, as `dup[\T\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `dup[\U\](x: Box[\U\])`; it refuses too a generic declaration beside one whose parameter types are its bounds, a plain one or a generic one whose parameter types mention none of its static parameters, 'fails because their parameter lists have the same types'. Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNoDuplicatesRule`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositions`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsPlain`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract` and `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstractSelfPositions`, the symbolic operator's case by `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsOperator`, walk's refusal by `tests/NoDuplicatesRuleWalk`, and those two refusals by `tests/GenericBesidePlainSameDomain` and `GenericBesideGenericSameDomain`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md` section 4, its `SKEPTIC.md` section 2, `compile-ladder/rung-duplicates-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 8, and `compile-ladder/rung-checker-abstract-callsite/REPORT.md` section 1.

- F-271 **The type group's POPL 2019 paper gives P-48's instance rule, and its soundness proof does not cover the library's F-bounded functions, such as `SUM` and `BIG MAX`.** By P-48's rule, a type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes the intersection of its upper bounds. The paper is later than both the specification and the team's restart (F-166). Its calculus does not let a method type parameter occur in an upper bound, so F-bounded method parameters are outside it. It also leaves out top-level functions and functional methods, among other limits. `reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md` checks the curator's decisions against the paper. Detail: `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md` sections 6 and 8.

- F-272 **The coercion example of the specification's "Coercion Resolution", over its own traits `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ128`, declares the exclusions that the chapter's definitions need: `ZZ32 excludes { ZZ64, ZZ128 }` and `ZZ64 excludes { ZZ128 }`.** A type `T` rejects `U` when every type that coerces to `T` excludes `U`. `T` is no less specific than `U` when it is a subtype of `U`, or excludes, coerces to and rejects it. So the choice of the more specific declaration depends on the exclusions. In the rung's probe, with the traits renamed `S32`, `S64` and `S128`, since the first two names are the library's, the revised example ran on both paths: `f(S32Of)`, on an `S32` value, chose `f` on `S64` and gave 1. No gated test runs the printed example. Row 394, fixed, names `tests/CoercionMostSpecificRungC.fss`, a walk test of the choice of the more specific coercion over three traits of the example's shape, each of which excludes both others. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md` section 4, decision 6; `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:558-574` (the definitions) and `:641` onward (the example).

- F-273 **The specification gives the run-time instance of a generic declaration that dispatch reaches, and that the static call did not select, by the POPL 2019 paper's rule.** It builds P-48. A declaration that the static call selected runs at the instance inferred for the call (F-173). Where an argument's value fixes a type parameter, as a value of `Tag[\X\]` fixes `X`, the rule and both paths agree. Where a type parameter is a parameter's whole type, the argument's run-time type only bounds it from below. The rule then gives it its declared bound, narrowed by what the call's static type requires of the return type. The dispatch paragraph's callout says that both paths take the argument's run-time type there instead. Walk always will, since it has no static types (P-48). The compiled path does so because its dispatcher is not given the call's static type (row 538, the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXGenericInstanceUnfixed`). The callout also says that the compiled path does not yet run the paragraph's second example, a generic declaration beside a plain one, reached through an argument of static type `Any` (row 496). Detail: `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:312-349`, in the chapter "Overloading and Multiple Dispatch"; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 5 and 6.

- F-300 **The type group's POPL 2019 paper, its technical report and the report's LaTeX sources are in `Papers/Variance/`.** The paper, Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance" (POPL 2019, doi:10.1145/3290324), is `3290324-popl19w.pdf`, under the CC BY-NC 4.0 licence that its first page prints. The technical report, the paper extended with the formalization in its appendices, is `3290324-popl19-TR.pdf`; the report and its sources (`paper.tex` and the files it reads) are included with Sukyoung Ryu's permission, and the report prints no licence of its own. ACM's `acmart.cls` and `ACM-Reference-Format.bst` there carry ACM's own terms. The working notes on the paper, its full text and its talk's transcript stay in `research/extracts/`. Read in the tree. Detail: `Papers/Variance/README.md`, "Permission and licence".

- F-319 **A comparison at a NaN or at 0/0 answers `false`, on the specification's word too.** It builds P-159. The overview of operators says that `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` return `false` at a floating-point NaN and at the rational 0/0, that `CMP` returns `Unordered` at a NaN, and that -1/0 and 1/0 are ordered below and above every finite rational (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex`, "Comparisons Operators"; Appendix I, "A comparison at a NaN or at the rational indefinite"); walk answers so, and the compiled path at a NaN (its library has no `CMP` on floats); nothing raises `FloatingComparisonError` or `RationalComparisonError`, which stay declared. Walk departs at 0/0 against itself, `true` for `=`, `<=` and `>=` and `EqualTo` for `CMP` (row 440). The team's later restart, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Operators/operator-overview.tick`, still says both comparisons raise: the rung that revised `Specification/` left it as the team wrote it, outside its files (climb batch 26's rung S). Test: `tests/ComparisonAtNaNWalk`, and the NaN asserts of `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyFloatCompiled` and `NativeHelperFamilyRR32Compiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-nan-comparison/REPORT.md` sections 1, 2 and 7.

- F-345 **The specification states, in the revision form, the static numerals (P-174, P-176) and P-171's string literals.** The literals chapter gives a numeral a numeral type that exists only at compile time, `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]` or `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` below a `Numeral` without static parameters, the four numbers its static arguments, naturals of any size, and every number type's coercion generic over the four numbers, each converted where it stands, and folded, one value per place. It also gives the conversion where a place fixes a type and the default elsewhere; a program's type receiving a numeral as written, its minus on the coercion's result, any other static expression through its coercion from the default's type; a `where` clause over the four numbers refusing statically; and the numeral types written only as parameter types (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:98-302`). The constant chapter gives the fold, converted from its exact value at a library type (`constant.tex:80-126`). The numbers chapter gives the coercions, with no `=` pairs and no `asFloat` on a numeral type (`basic-lib/numbers.tex:47-71`). The binary chapter's numeral declarations are expressible now and left out. Appendix I gives `revival-numerals`, `revival-numeral-numbers` and `revival-string-literals` (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), whose Effects name each departure of the two implementations with its row. Test: the specification's build (`ant genSource`, `ant tex`), 0 warnings by the skill's grep. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-static-numerals-spec/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- F-359 **The prelude's built-in number types were objects when first written, and became traits to nest them and to hold the literal objects; both reasons are gone from both libraries.** `object ZZ32 extends Number`, with `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64`, is of 2009-03-03 (`b2880c05c2`, Flood), the shape of the interpreter's library. They became traits on 2009-03-30 (`76c267f987`, Maessen: `trait ZZ32 extends ZZ64`, `object IntLiteral extends ZZ32`), and stayed traits when Chase flattened the tower (`6896886fbc`, 2009-08-31); the later built-in types followed the pattern. Chase's paper on the mapping calls the hand-written classes that carry these traits at run time, such as `FZZ32`, special cases "for the time being" (`Papers/Implementation/TypeMapping.tex:91-92`), and gives as the rule that a trait is an interface and an object a final class. His plan for unboxing (`compiler/optimization/Unbox.java`) is written over objects and `comprises` clauses and has no case for an open trait. So the trait form of a type that a hand-written class carries is later in date for every type, and the sources do not settle whether it is a decision of the team's in the sense of P-26. Read in the history and the texts. Command: `git log --full-history --reverse -S'object ZZ32' a874948ac -- ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`. Detail: `reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md`, "What the team's texts say, by provenance".

- F-371 **The team's texts describe no inference of the types that a declaration leaves out, beyond copying them from the exported api; for a method's types taken from the declaration that it implements, the Working Draft holds one sentence and two printed examples, and no rule.** The examples are `catalyze(reaction)` in trait `Enzyme`, with the sentence that it implements `Catalyst`'s abstract method, and `append(xs)` in object `Cons`. The Working Draft's chapter on whole-program inference is a heading and notes (F-169, on static-argument inference, reads the same chapter). The 2012 restart's chapter is a heading, and the type group's papers, the POPL 2019 paper among them, infer only a call's type arguments and write every parameter type. So row 405's gap, and a parameter whose type only its uses could give, as in the overview's `f(x) = x^2 + sin x - cos 2 x`, have no design of the team to build: a citation for them cites examples, not a rule. Evidence: read in the specification, the restart and `Papers/`; not searched: the 2012 patents, the printed versions 1.0 alpha and beta, and an email of 2007 that the draft's note cites. Detail: `explorations/reviews/omitted-types-intent-2026-11-16.md`, "What the designers' texts and code say" and "The team's own examples that leave types out".
